1275.title: the Sama Veda as song
1275.hook: the Chandogya Upanishad, a text of the Sama Veda, follows a chain from the ground under your feet to the high chant, link by link
1275.howItsDone: The Chandogya Upanishad, part of the Sama Veda's tradition, opens by teaching meditation on Om as the udgitha, the high chant, and is studied in Vedanta and recited in Vedic learning.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda: verses from the Rig Veda set to melody, opening with come, Agni, to the feast.
screen: `SAMAN: THE VERSE, SUNG.`

segments.voice: Orange juice in a carton. Before that, oranges in a crate. Before that, a tree; before that, rain and soil. Every glass at breakfast sits at the end of a chain nobody follows back. One old text follows a chain like that, link by link, from the ground up, but it isn't tracing breakfast. It's tracing a song. The Chandogya Upanishad belongs to the Sama Veda, and right at its start it asks what the very best part of everything is, and keeps going until it reaches the chant itself.
screen: `A GLASS OF JUICE, A CHAIN BEHIND IT.` → `ONE TEXT TRACES A SONG.` → `THE CHAIN THAT ENDS IN A CHANT.`

segments.voice: The Chandogya opens with the udgitha, the high chant, the part of a Sama Veda song the lead singer sends up. It says, in paraphrase: let a person meditate on the syllable Om as the udgitha, for the chant begins with Om. Then comes the chain. The essence of all beings is the earth. The essence of the earth is water. Of water, plants. Of plants, the human being. Of the human being, speech. Of speech, the Rig Veda's verses. Of the Rig Veda, the saman, the melody. And of the saman, the udgitha, which is Om. Walk it slowly: the ground, the rain in it, what grows from the rain, the people fed by it, their voices, the best words a voice can say, those words sung, and at the heart of the singing, one syllable. Each link is the rasa, the juice, the essence, of the one before. So in this picture a song isn't a pleasant extra laid on top of the words. It's what the words are reaching toward. And Om sits at the end of a line that starts with dirt. The Upanishad doesn't float the sacred syllable above ordinary things. It grows it from soil, water and food, through a body and a voice. Every Om, in this reading, has a field behind it.
screen: `THE UDGITHA: THE HIGH CHANT.` · `EARTH, WATER, PLANTS, PEOPLE, SPEECH.` · `VERSE, THEN MELODY, THEN OM.` · `EVERY OM HAS A FIELD BEHIND IT.`

segments.voice: Feel the ground under you, then the water in you, then the last thing you ate, grown somewhere, then yourself here, a person, walking the chain link by link. Let a quiet sound come on the out-breath, a hum, a word, or Om if you use it, and rest in the quiet after it before going around again. If you pray, rest in prayer at the end.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, the melody is the essence of the verse, and the high chant's heart is Om. Today's word.

1276.title: the Sama Veda as song
1276.hook: the gods and the demons were at war, and the gods reached for a song. the Chandogya tells which breath could carry it
1276.howItsDone: The story of the gods, the demons and the breath is taught from the second section of the Chandogya Upanishad, part of the Sama Veda's tradition, where the high chant is meditated on as the main breath, prana.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda as song, and the Chandogya's chain: earth, water, plants, people, speech, verse, melody, and at the end the high chant, Om.
screen: `FROM THE GROUND UP TO OM.`

segments.voice: The gods and the demons were at war. That's how the story starts, in the second section of the Chandogya Upanishad. Both sides are children of the same creator; both want to win. And the gods decide their weapon will be a song. Not a spear, not a trick: the udgitha, the high chant. With this, they say, we'll overcome them. But a chant needs something to carry it, so the gods try one part of a person after another, and the demons follow them to each. Today: which breath can hold the song.
screen: `THE GODS AND THE DEMONS AT WAR.` → `THE GODS REACH FOR A SONG.` → `WHAT CAN CARRY IT?`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, it goes like this. First the gods sing the chant as the breath in the nose. The demons pierce it with evil, and that, the text says, is why we smell both the sweet and the foul. Next, speech. Pierced: that's why we speak both truth and falsehood. Then the eye, and we see both what's fitting and what isn't. Then the ear, and we hear both. Then the mind, and we think both kinds of thoughts. Try after try, each one cracks, because each goes both ways. Then the gods sing the chant as the breath in the mouth, the main breath, the one that keeps a body alive. The demons rush at it and scatter, the text says, the way a lump of earth flung at a solid rock breaks into pieces. It's an explanation of everyday life, almost funny in its plainness: here's why your nose finds bad smells and your tongue tells lies. Every sense in us is mixed. But underneath them is a breath that simply keeps going, in and out, on good days and bad, choosing nothing. That breath is prana, and the Chandogya says the high chant is sung as it. The singer's song rides on the same breath that keeps the singer alive. In this reading, the Sama Veda isn't sung from the senses, or even from the mind first. It's sung from the breath.
screen: `NOSE, SPEECH, EYE, EAR, MIND: PIERCED.` · `EACH ONE GOES BOTH WAYS.` · `THE MAIN BREATH: THE DEMONS SCATTER.` · `THE SONG RIDES ON PRANA.`

segments.voice: Notice a smell in the room, a sound, what your eyes rest on, a thought passing, each with its own mood. Then let them all go and find the plain breath moving through mouth and throat, without controlling it, and when a sense pulls you away, come back to it. If you pray, let that breath carry your prayer.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, the high chant can't be carried by the senses or the mind. It's sung as the main breath, prana. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: the Sama Veda as song. Under every mixed sense, a breath that keeps going. See you tomorrow.

1277.title: the Sama Veda as song
1277.hook: na na na, hey hey. songs everywhere carry syllables that mean nothing. the Sama Veda's chants have them too, and the Chandogya gives them a world
1277.howItsDone: In Sama Veda chanting, the words of a verse are stretched and repeated and joined by syllables called stobhas, and the chants are learned from a teacher by ear.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda as song, and the gods' search for what could carry the high chant: every sense went both ways, and the main breath held.
screen: `THE SONG RIDES ON THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Na na na na. Hey hey. Ooh, la la. Plenty of songs have a stretch where the words run out and the singer keeps going anyway. Nobody looks those syllables up. And yet a crowd of strangers will sing them back, louder than the verses. Sama Veda chant has syllables like that too, sounds slipped between the words of the verse to carry the melody. A reader could skip them as filler. The Chandogya Upanishad doesn't. Today: the sounds between the words.
screen: `NA NA NA. HEY HEY.` → `NOT IN ANY DICTIONARY.` → `THE SOUNDS BETWEEN THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: When a verse becomes a saman, a Sama Veda chant, the words don't stay as they were. Vowels stretch. Syllables repeat. And between them come extra sounds, with names like hau and hai and auhoyi. These are stobhas. On their own they don't mean anything the way a word does; they're there for the song. Then the Chandogya gives the stobhas the world. In paraphrase: this world is the sound hau. The wind is hai. The moon is atha. And it goes on down a list, pairing chant-sounds with fire, with the sun, with breath, with food. So the sounds a hurried listener would call filler, the Upanishad treats as the places where the whole world comes into the song: earth, wind, moon, riding in syllables with no dictionary meaning. Readers take this more than one way. Some hear a meditation, a way for the singer to hold the whole world in mind while chanting. Some hear a deeper point about sound: meaning isn't only in what a word says, but in what a sound can hold. The Chandogya doesn't settle it. It just refuses to throw the small sounds away. And ordinary days are full of stobhas: the hmm while a friend talks, the oh when someone hands you coffee, the sigh at the end of a long day. Nothing in a dictionary. Not nothing.
screen: `STRETCHED, REPEATED, FILLED IN.` · `STOBHAS: HAU, HAI, AUHOYI.` · `THIS WORLD IS HAU. THE WIND IS HAI.` · `THE SMALL SOUNDS ARE NOT THROWN AWAY.`

segments.voice: On the out-breath let a soft open sound come, like haa or hau, quiet enough that no one else hears, just a sound with no meaning. On the next breaths make the same sound and let it hold one thing each time, the ground under you, the air in the room; if silence suits the place you're in, make the sound inside. If you pray, let it be prayer.
The Sama Veda as song. In the chant, small sounds called stobhas carry the melody, and the Chandogya pairs them with the world. Today's word.

1278.title: the Sama Veda as song
1278.hook: three singers sit down to talk shop, and one keeps asking: what holds that up? the answer goes all the way to space
1278.howItsDone: The dialogue of Shilaka, Dalbhya and King Pravahana is taught from the Chandogya Upanishad, part of the Sama Veda's tradition, as a meditation on the high chant resting finally on space.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda as song, and the stobhas: small sounds between the words, which the Chandogya pairs with earth, wind and moon.
screen: `THE SOUNDS BETWEEN THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Why is the sky blue? Because of the light. Why? Because of the air. Why? Small children play this at bedtime, and the questions stop only when someone runs out of answers, or patience. The Chandogya Upanishad tells a story that runs like that. Three men skilled in the high chant of the Sama Veda sit down to talk about it, two brahmins and a king. And one question keeps getting asked, each time one step further down: what does that rest on?
screen: `WHY? BECAUSE. WHY?` → `THREE SINGERS SIT DOWN TOGETHER.` → `WHAT HOLDS UP A SONG?`

segments.voice: Their names are Shilaka, Dalbhya and Pravahana. Pravahana, the king, says: you two speak first; I'll listen. So Shilaka asks Dalbhya, in paraphrase: what does the saman, the chant, rest on? Dalbhya says: on tone, the sound of the voice. And tone? On breath. And breath? On food. And food? On water. And water? On that world, the heavens. And the heavens? Here Dalbhya stops. We don't lead the chant past the heavens, he says; we set it there. Shilaka isn't satisfied. The heavens, he says, rest on this world, the earth beneath us. Then Shilaka puts the question to the king: and this world, what does it rest on? Pravahana's answer: on space. All beings come out of space and go back into space, he says. Space is greater than all of them, the last support. And that, he says, is the high chant at its best: without end. Look at the shape of it. A song rests on a voice, the voice on breath, the breath on food, the food on water, and on down until the floor under everything is open room, not a thing but the space things happen in. A note only rings because there's air and room around it; sing into a pillow and it dies. It took three people, patience, and one more question to get there.
screen: `TWO BRAHMINS AND A KING.` · `TONE, BREATH, FOOD, WATER, HEAVEN.` · `AND THE EARTH? IT RESTS ON SPACE.` · `A NOTE RINGS BECAUSE THERE IS ROOM.`

segments.voice: At the end of each out-breath there's a small pause before the next breath comes; let your attention rest there without stretching it. Then listen for the quiet between one sound and the next, and the gap after a passing thought, the open room everything else happens in. If you pray, rest in prayer there.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, three singers ask what the chant rests on: tone, breath, food, water, heaven, earth, and at last, space. Today's word.

1279.title: the Sama Veda as song
1279.hook: a book of songs, Indra, the mind, awareness: one line of the Gita holds them together
1279.howItsDone: In the Gita's tenth chapter Krishna names where he can be found, including 'of the Vedas, I am the Sama Veda', and the Sama Veda itself is kept by chanters who learn it by ear.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda as song, and three singers asking what the chant rests on, down through breath, food and earth, until a king answered: space.
screen: `THE CHANT RESTS ON SPACE.`

segments.voice: A book of songs. Indra, among the gods. The mind. Awareness. They share a single line of the Bhagavad Gita. This path has been in that chapter before, the tenth, where Krishna said, among meters, I am the Gayatri. Earlier in the same list, he names something this week has been listening to. After days of chants, breath and stobhas, it may not be a surprise what. Today, the last day on the Sama Veda: what Krishna says about it.
screen: `SONGS, INDRA, THE MIND, AWARENESS.` → `ONE LINE OF THE GITA.` → `AMONG THE VEDAS, ONE.`

segments.voice: Arjuna has asked how he should think of Krishna, and Krishna answers with a list: in each kind of thing, one where he can be found. Among lights, the sun. Today's verse, Gita ten, twenty-two, begins: vedanam samavedo 'smi. Of the Vedas, I am the Sama Veda. Then, in the same breath: among the gods, I am Indra. Among the senses, the mind. In living beings, awareness. That's the whole line. The Gita doesn't stop to explain why the Sama Veda; it says it and moves on. So readers have wondered. Some point to what we've seen these days. The Sama Veda is the Rig Veda's verses, sung: the words are the same, and what's added is melody. And in his list Krishna keeps naming the one in each group where something shines through. A verse sung is still the verse, but now it rings. Some readers also notice the company it keeps: Indra, the god of last week's hymns; the mind, which gathers what the senses bring; awareness, the light by which any of it is known. That's a lot of honor for a melody. Remember the Chandogya's chain: the essence of speech is the verse, and the essence of the verse is the chant. Some hear Krishna's line landing in the same place from another direction: what is holy in the words comes through when they're sung. Arjuna's question still works on an ordinary day. Where should I look for you? One answer this verse gives: wherever something is being sung.
screen: `OF THE VEDAS, I AM THE SAMA VEDA.` · `THE GITA DOESN'T SAY WHY.` · `BESIDE INDRA, THE MIND, AWARENESS.` · `THE WORDS, SUNG, BEGIN TO RING.`

segments.voice: Close or soften your eyes and listen outward, traffic, a fan, a bird, a voice somewhere, the hum of a fridge, without naming anything. Then ask Arjuna's question gently, where should I look, and let your attention rest on whichever sound feels most like singing, or on your own breath if none does. If you pray, rest in prayer there.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Gita, Krishna says: of the Vedas, I am the Sama Veda, the Veda that is sung. Today's word.

1280.title: the Atharva Veda's healing hymns
1280.hook: turmeric in warm milk at a sick child's bedside. one Veda turns from the great fire altar to rooms like that one
1280.howItsDone: The Atharva Veda holds hymns for healing fever, wounds and broken bones, often said together with a healing plant; its recitation is kept by Vedic chanters of its own schools.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-EIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the Sama Veda, with Krishna in the Gita: of the Vedas, I am the Sama Veda.
screen: `OF THE VEDAS, THE ONE THAT IS SUNG.`

segments.voice: A saucepan on low heat. Milk, a spoon of turmeric, maybe a pinch of pepper, stirred until it goes gold. Then down the hall to a kid in bed with a cough and a warm forehead. In some homes that cup is a remedy handed down from grandparents. Nobody calls it scripture; it's just what you do when someone you love is sick. The Vedas we've read so far mostly stand at the great fire altar, with priests, hymns and melodies. The Atharva Veda walks down the hall, with hymns for fevers, wounds and broken bones. Today: the Veda of remedies.
screen: `TURMERIC IN WARM MILK.` → `DOWN THE HALL TO A SICK BED.` → `THE VEDA OF REMEDIES.`

segments.voice: The Atharva Veda's word for a remedy is bheshaja: medicine, cure, what makes well. It runs all through these hymns. Some are addressed to fever, some to plants, some to a wound or an aching limb. The healer speaks, the plant is given, and the hymn says what the healing should do. Listen to one, a hymn for setting a broken bone. In paraphrase: let marrow come together with marrow, joint with joint. Let what has fallen away of the flesh, and the bone too, grow back. It isn't abstract. It names the body part by part, the way a person setting a bone would have to think: marrow, joint, flesh, bone, and it speaks a hope over each, that it knit. A plant goes with it. The hymn speaks to a healing herb and calls it rohani, the grower of the broken bone. So the hymn isn't a prayer floating above the injury. It's said right at the injury, alongside the herb. That's the turn the Atharva Veda makes. The Vedas this path has heard so far sing to the gods at the great rites. This one also sits at the bedside and speaks to a fever, a cut, a bone, as places where the sacred is needed too. Here an aching body is not too ordinary to be spoken over, and caring for one is not small.
screen: `BHESHAJA: A REMEDY, A CURE.` · `MARROW TO MARROW, JOINT TO JOINT.` · `SAID AT THE INJURY, WITH THE HERB.` · `A BODY IS NOT TOO ORDINARY.`

segments.voice: Move your attention part by part, the way the hymn does: feet, knees, hips, back, shoulders, hands, jaw. Find one place that aches or feels tight and stay with it kindly, without fixing it, the way someone sits at a bedside, breathing toward it. If you pray, hold that place, or someone who is sick, in prayer.
The Atharva Veda's healing hymns. Bheshaja, remedy: hymns spoken at the bedside over fever, wound and bone. Today's word.
screen: `THE ATHARVA VEDA'S HEALING HYMNS — today's word`.

1281.title: the Atharva Veda's healing hymns
1281.hook: "homage to the cold fever." it sounds like a line for a god. an Atharva Veda hymn says it to a sickness
1281.howItsDone: The Atharva Veda's hymns to takman, fever, address the sickness directly, naming its origin and its forms, offering it homage and asking it to depart; they belong to the Atharva Veda's healing hymns.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Atharva Veda's healing hymns: bheshaja, remedy, and a hymn for a broken bone, marrow to marrow, joint to joint.
screen: `MARROW TO MARROW, JOINT TO JOINT.`

segments.voice: Homage to the cold fever. Homage to the burning one. Said aloud, it could be a line from a temple, offered to a god. It's said to a sickness. Anyone who has sat up at night beside someone burning and shivering may have muttered at the fever itself: go away, leave them alone. The Atharva Veda has hymns that speak to fever like that, as if it can hear. And one of them, before it asks the fever to leave, bows.
screen: `HOMAGE TO THE COLD FEVER.` → `SAID TO A SICKNESS.` → `THE HYMN THAT BOWS TO IT.`

segments.voice: The Atharva Veda's word for fever is takman, and in these hymns takman is spoken to like a someone, not a something. One hymn begins by naming where the fever comes from. In paraphrase: when fire entered the waters and burned, there, they say, is your birthplace. So the healer starts by knowing the fever's family: it came from fire. Then the hymn names its shapes. The cold fever. The burning one. The fever that comes back the next day, and the one that comes back on the third: the shaking, the heat, the false hope of a good afternoon. Then the line from the start of today. Homage to the cold fever. Homage to the burning one. Namah: the same word people use to bow to a god, said to a sickness. Why bow to it? The hymn doesn't explain. One reading: the healer treats the fever as a power to be respected and then asked to leave, not just cursed. Another: you name a thing fully, honor its strength, and only then send it off. Either way, the hymn doesn't pretend the fever is small. That's been the thread this week. The Chandogya grew the high chant from earth and breath. Three singers found the song resting on space. Krishna named the Sama Veda as his own. And the Atharva Veda brings that same care for words to a sickbed. Marrow to marrow. Homage to the fever. Now go.
screen: `TAKMAN: FEVER, SPOKEN TO.` · `BORN WHERE FIRE ENTERED THE WATERS.` · `COLD, BURNING, COMING BACK.` · `HOMAGE TO THE FEVER, THEN: GO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time you were sick and someone stayed, a parent, a partner, a roommate, a nurse whose name you never learned, and see the room: the cloth, the glass of water, the voice in the dark. Let thanks rise toward them, whether they're near or far or gone, and if someone you know is sick now, hold them too, the way you were once held. If you pray, pray for them.
The Atharva Veda's healing hymns. Takman, fever: named by its birthplace and its shapes, honored, and asked to go. Today's word.
